content:
The night the body turned up in the Limmat was cold and damp, the kind that seeps into your bones like cheap whiskey. It was late October, and the city had that particular Zurich fog that clings to the edges of the streets like smoke. I was patrolling the riverbank, the paving stones slick with drizzle, when something caught my eye—something that didn't belong to the usual ghostly shapes and shadows of the Limmat at this hour.

The body was a man, middle-aged, his clothes wrong for the water—too clean, too expensive, torn open like a dressmaker had ripped something apart. His face... no face. The river had taken it. I stood there for a while, watching the current carry his clothes downstream, thinking how strange it was that a man like this would come to the Limmat looking like he'd just stepped out of a bank vault into a storm.

That's how you find your cases in Zurich. You don't look for them—you trip over them when the city decides to hand them to you on a silver platter wrapped in fog and regret.
